newsitem.title: USA: German officials say talk of EMU delay premature.
newsitem.headline: German officials say talk of EMU delay premature.

text.p: An official from the German finance ministry and a Bundesbank council member both said on Thursday that recent speculation about a delay in the launch of a single European currency was premature.

"I do not think any second of a delay because our projects are so important," said Bundesbank council member Wendelin Hartmann. "For those who have to do the work a delay or a postponement is not a point of discussion."

Hartmann, along with German Ministry of Finance official Juergen Stark and other experts, spoke to the press in New York before a discussion on European economic and monetary union sponsored by the Council on Foreign Relations and Deutsche Bank AG.
Stark voiced optimism that European Union member countries still had time to meet strict Maastricht criteria, despite recent talk in the financial markets that a postponement could be forthcoming.
"We have still 12 months to go and still 12 months to work," said Stark, who is State Secretary within the Ministry.
In discussing the selection of the starting members of monetary union in a speech, Stark took a hard line, saying "The criteria for being part of the first round are clear and will have to be met."

"Political compromises are out of the question when the trademark of our new currency, namely stability insulated from political interference, shall have the slightest credibility in international markets," he added.

Stark said German government forecasts for a government deficit of less than 3.0 percent of GDP in 1997 still stand and have not been jeopardized by "strongly seasonally influenced unemployment numbers."
All the panelists stressed that the costs of a delay in EMU were enormous from both a political and a financial perspective.
"It is our perception that the resolve is there," said Ronaldo Schmitz, a member of the board of managing directors at Deutsche Bank AG.
Asked when he foresaw a pickup in domestic consumption, Stark suggested it could be around the corner.
"At present economic growth is mainly export led," he conceded. "But we expect that during the spring and early summer there will be a spillover effect to private consumption."
Both Hartmann and Stark said the dollar's rise from post-World War II lows against the deutschemark represented a "normalization" of exchange rates.

"The present level of dollar/mark reflects more or less the real economic situation in both countries," said Hartmann. "What we have had is a normalization. An exchange rate of 1.70 in dollar/mark is quite acceptable."
On Thursday, the dollar ended the day at 1.7055 marks, up from 1.6928 on Wednesday.
